content: Hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are a corticosteroid medication designed for rectal use. They are primarily indicated for the treatment of inflamed hemorrhoids, post-irradiation proctitis, chronic ulcerative colitis (as an adjunct therapy), cryptitis, and other inflammatory conditions of the anorectal region, including pruritus ani. The medication works by reducing inflammation, itching, and irritation in the affected areas. To administer the suppository, one should carefully detach a single suppository from the strip, remove the wrapper, and avoid excessive handling to prevent premature melting. For nonspecific proctitis, the recommended dosage is one suppository inserted twice daily, in the morning and at night, for a duration of two weeks. In more severe cases, the dosage may be increased to one suppository three times daily or two suppositories twice daily. For post-irradiation proctitis, treatment duration typically ranges from six to eight weeks, depending on the patient’s response. Hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to hydrocortisone acetate or any of the product’s components. Before initiating treatment, a thorough proctologic examination is necessary. If irritation or adverse reactions occur, the medication should be discontinued, and alternative therapy should be considered. In cases of concurrent infection, appropriate antifungal or antibacterial agents should be used. If the infection does not respond promptly, hydrocortisone acetate should be discontinued until the infection is adequately controlled. Commonly reported adverse reactions include burning, itching, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, hypopigmentation, allergic contact dermatitis, and secondary infections. These reactions are typically localized to the site of application. The safety of hydrocortisone acetate suppositories during pregnancy is not well established. Animal studies have shown an increased risk of fetal abnormalities with topical steroid use at low doses. Therefore, this medication should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefits outweigh the risks to the fetus. It is not known whether hydrocortisone acetate is excreted in human breast milk. Given the potential for serious adverse effects in nursing infants, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the medication, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. There is limited information regarding the use of hydrocortisone acetate suppositories in pediatric, geriatric, or immunocompromised patients, as well as in individuals with renal or hepatic impairment. Similarly, there is no specific guidance on its use in relation to gender or racial populations. Approximately 26% of hydrocortisone acetate is absorbed when applied rectally in healthy individuals. Absorption may vary in cases of abraded or inflamed rectal tissue. The therapeutic effects of hydrocortisone acetate are primarily due to its anti-inflammatory, anti-pruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties. Hydrocortisone acetate suppositories are supplied in boxes of 12 or 24 units, with each suppository containing 25 mg of the active ingredient. They should be stored at temperatures between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F) and protected from freezing. This medication requires a prescription for dispensing. Patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding the use of alcohol while on this medication, as no established interaction data is available. Additionally, patients should be informed about the proper administration technique and potential side effects of the medication.
